# Finite speed of light (`speed_of_light`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by telescope, pendulum_clock, astronomical_distances, heliocentrism
- Core idea: Light is not instantaneous; it travels about 300,000 km per second, so it takes a little over a second from the Moon and about eight minutes from the Sun. First evidence: the eclipses of Jupiter's innermost moon come later than the timetable when the Earth is moving away from Jupiter and earlier when it approaches, in total by about 17 minutes across the Earth's orbit, the time light needs to cross it. On Earth it can be measured with a rapidly spinning toothed wheel or mirror and a mirror several kilometres away.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying Galileo's lantern test between hills (human reaction time is millions of times too slow)
  - Saying Rømer measured the speed: he showed it is finite; a value needs the size of the Earth's orbit
  - Quoting 300,000 km per hour or per minute
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Empedocles holds that light takes time; Aristotle denies it; islamic: 11th c. – Ibn al-Haytham and al-Biruni argue for a finite speed; europe: 1638 Galileo proposes a lantern test; 1676 Rømer's delay of Io's eclipses (Huygens derives about 220,000 km/s); 1728 Bradley's aberration of starlight; 1849 Fizeau's toothed wheel, 1862 Foucault's rotating mirror (298,000 km/s); americas: 1879–1926 – Michelson's precision measurements
- Read:
  - Ole Rømer, Démonstration touchant le mouvement de la lumière, Journal des Sçavans (1676)
  - John C. H. Spence, Lightspeed: The Ghostly Aether and the Race to Measure the Speed of Light (2019)
